oni.desc: The Oceanic Niño Index — 3-month running mean of Niño 3.4 SST anomalies, the official ENSO yardstick. +0.5°C sustained = El Niño.
oni.inference: The ONI has now cleared the El Niño threshold and is accelerating. The March–May reading was +0.48°C; the latest season is near +0.9°C and climbing, with the slope steepening rather than flattening. This is the trajectory of a sustained event, not a stall — the curve now resembles 1997 and 2015 far more than the 2023 peak-and-fade the spring analysis flagged as the downside case. Because ONI is a 3-month mean it lags the weekly Niño 3.4 (already +1.7°C), so the official index will keep rising mechanically over the coming months even before further warming.

roni.desc: The Relative ONI strips out the long-term warming baseline. In a warmer mean ocean, ONI runs hot — RONI is the more honest measure of physical strength.
roni.inference: The ONI–RONI gap persists at roughly 0.3°C — the warming-baseline signature. This matters for how the peak should be read: an event that prints as 'very strong' on absolute ONI may be physically closer to 'strong' once the baseline is removed, which tempers the most extreme record-chasing forecasts. But the direction is unambiguous — RONI has now crossed into positive territory alongside ONI, confirming the warming is a genuine ENSO signal and not merely the background trend. Watch whether RONI continues to converge toward ONI as the event matures.

nino34.desc: Niño 3.4 weekly SST anomaly — the fastest-moving surface signal. Momentum foreshadows whether the event is accelerating into the threshold.
nino34.inference: This is the chart that resolved the spring's central question. Niño 3.4 has climbed from +0.5°C in late May to +1.7°C by mid-June — a +1.5°C three-month move, among the fastest on record and now within striking distance of the +2.0°C very-strong threshold. The momentum that in the spring 'could reverse fast' has instead compounded. ECMWF's early-July run suggests anomalies could top +3.0°C by autumn. The 2014-style stall the note warned about did not materialise; the June easterly burst that deferred 2014 to 2015 has no analogue this cycle.

subsurface.desc: Warm Water Volume anomaly — the subsurface heat reservoir that fuels surface warming. A strong recharge is the precondition for a strong event.
subsurface.inference: The fuel gauge that read near-full in the spring has been drawn down into surface warming exactly as a developing event requires — subsurface heat is now feeding the surface rather than merely sitting in reserve. The reservoir remains deep enough to support a very strong peak, and unlike 2014, it has not been discharged prematurely by an easterly wind burst. The subsurface-to-surface handoff is proceeding cleanly, which is the mechanical signature of an event that will sustain into its autumn–winter peak.

atmosphere.desc: SOI and trade winds confirm whether the atmosphere is coupling to the ocean. Sustained negative SOI plus weakening trades = the Bjerknes feedback locking in.
atmosphere.inference: This was the decisive uncertainty in the spring, and it has resolved to the upside. The atmosphere has coupled: SOI has fallen firmly negative, trade winds have weakened decisively, and thunderstorm activity has shifted to the central and eastern Pacific while suppressing over Indonesia — the textbook Bjerknes-feedback signature. The 2023-style 'coupling that never locked in' scenario is off the table. With ocean and atmosphere now reinforcing each other, the event has the self-sustaining structure that distinguishes a genuine strong-to-very-strong El Niño from a false start.

regime.name: ENSO Regime Score
regime.interp: Firmly in El Niño territory and rising. A full El Niño Advisory with a very-strong peak the modal outcome.

coupling.name: Atmospheric Coupling
coupling.interp: Locked in. SOI firmly negative, trades weakened, convection shifted to the central-eastern Pacific. The spring's decisive uncertainty has resolved to the upside.
